vignette: The rain never stops during the crossing. Arjun stands ankle-deep in mud, watching border guards' flashlights cut through the dark like searchlights from another life. He is twenty-two. The radio in his pocket crackles with static, then goes dead. He presses his father's face into his memory one last time before the soldiers separate the men. The next three years blur into a sequence of crowded tents, thin broth, and the constant calculation of which direction feels safest. Sleep becomes a currency he cannot afford. When he does close his eyes, the ground beneath him shifts, and he wakes with his heart hammering against his ribs, already braced for the next order to move. In the camp, survival means becoming invisible. Arjun learns to move through the periphery, to watch exits before entering rooms, to keep his hands visible and his voice low. When the resettlement papers finally arrive, the plane feels less like an escape and more like a suspended sentence. For a while, the quiet of his new country lulls him. He works odd jobs, pays rent, and lets the silence mask the noise in his head. But quiet is fragile. On a Tuesday evening, a car backfires two blocks from his apartment. The sound hits him like a physical blow. He drops to his knees behind the couch, breath coming in short, sharp pulls, until the smell of burnt toast from the neighboring kitchen finally pulls him back to the present. He does not call anyone. He waits until his hands stop shaking, then washes them until the skin cracks. Now, at forty-four, Arjun commands a professional kitchen. Heat, noise, and precise timing are his vocabulary. He runs the pass like a captain, calling tickets, adjusting heat, keeping the brigade in rhythm. The chaos of service should trigger him, but instead, it grounds him. Control is a recipe he knows how to follow. He arrives at 4 a.m. to inspect the delivery, checking each crate with meticulous care. He memorizes every cook who works his line, watching for the slightest tremor in a hand or a distracted glance. Cooking is the only time his mind stops racing. When the knives hit the cutting board in steady succession, when the oil smokes at the exact temperature he needs, the world narrows to the task at hand. He does not think about borders. He thinks about seasoning, about timing, about feeding people who will never ask where he has been. His apartment remains sparsely furnished. He keeps the doors locked, the windows drawn, the phone on silent. Women ask him out, but he lets the conversations fade, not out of indifference, but out of a quiet fear of entanglement. Intimacy feels like a risk he cannot calculate. At work, he is respected, almost mythical. The sous-chefs call him Bhai as a joke, but they also watch how he scans the room before seating staff, how he stops mid-sentence when a fire alarm tests at the wrong moment. He drinks his tea black, sits by the kitchen door during his breaks, and listens to the hum of the exhaust fans until his breathing matches their steady rhythm. Some days, the memories do not visit him-they live in his shoulders, in the tightness behind his eyes, in the way he flinches when a delivery truck reverses in the alley below. He tells himself this is just how men his age carry the weight of survival. He does not say that some nights, he sleeps in his uniform, one shoe on, one foot ready to run. The PCL-5 score of 42 would, on paper, map onto a clinical picture. Here, it is just the way he measures flour by touch, the way he avoids the alley after midnight, the way he keeps his jacket zipped even in July. When he walks to the market, he sticks to the main roads, his posture rigid, his eyes constantly tracking movement at street level. He eats alone at a corner table near the back of the restaurant, finishing his meal in minutes before excusing himself to the prep station. The kitchen is his sanctuary and his battleground. On rare quiet mornings, he stands at the sink and watches the water run, listening for footsteps in the stairwell that are not there. He does not fight the memories anymore. He has learned to let them pass like weather, knowing that if he stops moving, stops cooking, stops scanning the perimeter, the ground might shift again. He works the line. He calls the orders. He breathes. The fire stays contained within the burners.
